opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that gets me most excited is how general it is. With traditional tool use, someone has to sit down and build an integration for every single thing you want the model to touch: write the API wrapper, define the schema, handle auth, maintain it as the service changes. That works great for the handful of things that are worth that investment, but there's this enormous long tail of software out there that's never going to get a nice clean API. Think of internal enterprise tools, legacy desktop apps, random government websites, that kind of thing.

Computer use flips that around. The interface that every piece of software already exposes is the one built for humans: a screen, a mouse, and a keyboard. If the model can operate that interface, then suddenly it can use basically anything a person can use, without anyone having to build a bespoke tool first. So in a sense it's the universal tool, the one tool that unlocks all the others.

The other part I find compelling is how it changes the way people start using these systems. You don't have to be a developer who knows how to wire up function calling. You can say, "Here's how I do this task on my computer, go do it," and the model can follow along in the same environment you work in. That's much closer to how you'd onboard a new coworker.

To be clear, it's not always the best choice. If there's a good API, calling it directly is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than clicking around a GUI. The way I think about it is that computer use is the fallback that guarantees coverage. Use structured tools where they exist, and use computer use for everything else. As the models get better at perceiving screens and recovering from mistakes, that "everything else" bucket gets really powerful.

r001.rationale: It says computer use avoids building and maintaining a bespoke API wrapper, schema, and authentication flow for each integration, reducing integration engineering effort.

r002.rationale: It mentions non-developers using computer use, but does not explain integrating a customer support bot with systems through an authenticated browser.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing I find really compelling about computer use is that it's kind of the universal API. When you think about tool use today, every tool you want a model to use, somebody has to go write an integration for it. You define a schema, you write the function, you handle the errors, and you do that over and over for every single application. And there's this huge long tail of software out there that's never going to get a nice clean API. A ton of important work happens in legacy enterprise apps, in internal tools some company built ten years ago, in random websites that were only ever designed for a human sitting in front of a screen.

Computer use just sidesteps all of that. Humans built the entire digital world to be operated through a screen, a mouse, and a keyboard. If a model can see the screen and operate those same inputs, then in principle it can use any piece of software that a person can, without anyone writing a bespoke integration first. That's what gets me excited. It's not that clicking around a GUI is the most efficient way to do any particular task. For a lot of things, a direct API call is going to be faster and more reliable, and you should absolutely use it when it exists. It's that computer use is the fallback that covers everything else.

The other piece is that it's a really honest test of model capability. You can't hide behind a carefully designed tool interface. The model has to look at pixels, figure out what's on the screen, plan a multi-step sequence, click something, see what happened, and correct itself when it misclicks or a page loads slowly. That whole loop of acting, observing, and recovering is exactly the agentic behavior we care about more broadly. So when we were building this, it felt like working on computer use was pulling forward a lot of the general capabilities we'd want anyway.

And honestly, part of it is just that it was fun. The first time I watched the model open a browser, navigate somewhere, fill out a form, and actually finish the task, it felt qualitatively different from a chat response. It was doing a thing in the world. It's still early, it's slow, it makes mistakes, but the trajectory is pretty clear, and I think in a few years we'll look back and find it strange that we ever expected every tool to come with a hand-written integration.

r001.rationale: It says computer use can work across software without someone writing a bespoke integration, avoiding repeated per-application integration work.

r002.rationale: It does not describe non-engineering teams integrating a customer support bot through an authenticated browser.

astra-6.text:
What excites me about computer use is that it gives you a general interface to software. With traditional tool use, you have to expose an API, describe it to the model, and build an integration for each thing you want it to do. But we already have an interface that lets people use all of these tools: the screen, the mouse, and the keyboard.

If a model can use that interface, it can potentially work with software that nobody has built a special integration for. It can move between applications and carry out a workflow much like a person would.

I think APIs still make sense when you have them—they’re generally faster and more reliable. Computer use is exciting because it fills in the gaps. You don’t have to anticipate every tool the model might need before it can start doing useful work.

r001.rationale: It contrasts custom API exposure and building an integration for each tool with using the screen, mouse, and keyboard, explicitly saying this avoids special integrations.

r002.rationale: It does not mention teams without engineers, a customer support bot, authenticated browser access, or integrating with their systems.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is that computers are already the interface to almost everything we want an AI to do. With tool use, you typically have to build a specific integration: define the API, explain the inputs, and connect it to the model. That works really well, but there’s a lot of software that doesn’t have an API, or where the API only exposes part of what you can do in the product.

Computer use gives you a much more general interface. If the model can look at a screen and use a mouse and keyboard, it can potentially use the same software a person uses. You don’t have to build a new integration for every application.

And the interesting part is combining those approaches. Use an API when there’s a good one, use code when that’s the most efficient way to do something, and use the computer interface to fill in the gaps. That opens up a much wider range of tasks you can actually complete end to end.

r001.rationale: The response says computer use avoids building a new integration for every application, reducing the work required compared with custom API integrations.

r002.rationale: It does not describe non-engineering teams integrating a customer support bot with their systems through an authenticated browser.
